nameStory: This beetle gets its name from its favorite food: Saint John's wort, a yellow-flowered plant that blooms around Saint John's Day in late June. The beetle was actually brought to North America on purpose in the 1940s to help control this weedy plant that was taking over pastures and poisoning livestock.
description: The Saint John's wort beetle is a small, chunky leaf beetle about the size of a ladybug. Adults are metallic bronze to copper-colored with a glossy, almost mirror-like shine that catches the light beautifully. They have the typical rounded, dome-shaped body of leaf beetles, with short antennae and sturdy legs built for clinging to plant stems.

idTips.label: Metallic bronze color
idTips.description: Shiny copper to bronze coloration that looks almost like polished metal, much more reflective than most other small beetles

idTips.label: Host plant association
idTips.description: Almost always found on Saint John's wort plants, feeding on the bright yellow flowers and oval leaves

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About 6-7mm long, roughly ladybug-sized but more oval-shaped and less rounded than a ladybug

idTips.label: Feeding damage
idTips.description: Look for plants with holes chewed through leaves and flowers that appear ragged or skeletonized

idTips.label: Clustering behavior
idTips.description: Often found in small groups of 3-10 beetles feeding together on the same plant

habitat: Found in sunny, open areas where Saint John's wort grows, including roadsides, old fields, meadows, and disturbed soils. Common in both rural and suburban areas throughout New England, especially in well-drained soils where the host plant thrives.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge in late spring and begin feeding on young Saint John's wort shoots. Look for small holes appearing in fresh green leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both adults and larvae are actively feeding. Most easily spotted during July when Saint John's wort is in full bloom.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding into early fall before seeking shelter for winter. Feeding damage from the season is most visible on plants.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in leaf litter and under bark. Not visible during this season.

funFact: This beetle is one of nature's most successful biological control agents - it was deliberately imported from Europe and has been so effective at controlling Saint John's wort that the weedy plant went from covering millions of acres to being relatively rare in many areas!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small metallic leaf beetles, but the bronze color and exclusive association with Saint John's wort plants makes identification straightforward. Remember: bronze beetle, yellow flowers - they go together!
contextualKnowledge: This is actually a non-native species that most people consider beneficial because it controls a problematic weed. It's one of the few introduced insects that naturalists and farmers alike are happy to see in New England.
compareHints: Since this is the only Chrysolina species commonly found in New England, compare it to other metallic leaf beetles like Japanese beetles (which are larger and more golden) or flea beetles (which are much smaller and jump when disturbed). The Saint John's wort beetle's bronze color and medium size, plus its specific plant association, sets it apart from these relatives.
